analysis.one_liner: Puts a 0.1 percent tax on trades of stocks, bonds, and derivatives.
analysis.headline: The Wall Street Tax Act never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would place a small tax — 0.1 percent, or $1 on every $1,000 — on each purchase of stocks, bonds, and many derivatives [S2] [S3]. Initial stock offerings and very short-term debt would be exempt, and the tax would also reach trades routed through foreign subsidiaries controlled by U.S. owners, a common way to dodge U.S. taxes [S3]. The money would flow to the Treasury like any other federal tax. The bill was introduced in March 2019, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended [S5] [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the federal Treasury would collect revenue from high-volume financial trading, which is dominated by large banks, hedge funds, and trading firms. Ordinary investors would pay the tax only pennies at a time through fund trades, and retirement savers' accounts would feel only a small drag. The tax also reaches some offshore trading structured through controlled foreign corporations, closing a route wealthy investors use to avoid U.S. tax [S3] [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.1 percent excise tax on each purchase of stocks, bonds, and specified derivatives, with the tax collected by exchanges and brokers for transactions on U.S. venues [S3] [S2].
Exempts initial issues of securities and short-term debt maturing within 100 days, targeting the tax at secondary-market trading rather than companies raising capital [S3] [S2].

Treats controlled foreign corporations as U.S. persons for the tax and requires their U.S. shareholders to pay their share, limiting the ability to route trades through offshore subsidiaries [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large banks, hedge funds, high-frequency trading firms, and other heavy traders would bear the tax directly, and brokerage and asset-management firms would handle collection. Some of the cost would be passed through to ordinary investors in mutual funds and retirement accounts as slightly higher trading costs [S3] [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Big banks, hedge funds, and trading firms

drawbacks.text: Even a small per-trade tax compounds over millions of fund transactions, so some of the cost would land on ordinary investors through mutual funds and 401(k)-style accounts, and critics argue high-volume traders could shift activity to overseas venues, shrinking the revenue [S3].
The bill raises revenue but does not direct it to any specific program, so its benefit to any particular group of working people depends entirely on later spending decisions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is small on any single trade but falls overwhelmingly on high-volume traders, whose activity is dominated by large financial institutions; the design — exempting initial offerings and short-term debt, and covering offshore subsidiaries — shows an effort to aim the burden at speculative trading rather than capital-raising or everyday savers. The main honest cost is that some pass-through to ordinary fund investors is unavoidable, and revenue could erode if trading moved abroad. On balance it is a modest, well-targeted tax on a concentrated interest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2019 and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on March 5, 2019, joined by Democratic Sens. Van Hollen, Merkley, and Gillibrand [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the last action ever taken on it [S5] [S1].
The bill ended the Congress without a committee vote, a floor vote, or any recorded committee action [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms are better off, since they never faced the tax; the Senate Finance Committee's decision to take no action on the bill is what kept it off the floor. Ordinary taxpayers received no revenue from it.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2019 and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sens. Chris Van Hollen, Jeff Merkley, and Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: Cosponsors from Maryland, Oregon, and New York
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; it drew no additional cosponsors afterward.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the two years the chamber controlled the agenda.

sides.party_line_note: All four Senate backers were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; Republicans held a majority in the Senate and chaired the Finance Committee where the bill stalled.

industries.industry: Banks, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms
industries.note: These firms execute most of the high-volume trading the 0.1 percent tax would hit, so the tax is aimed squarely at their transaction costs. Their gain in avoiding it came at the cost of revenue that could have served taxpayers.

The bill makes exchanges and brokers the collectors of the tax and adds a cost layer to fund trading, part of which passes to ordinary investors. Their incentive to oppose the bill ran against the public's interest in the revenue.

U.S. exchanges would be responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on trades on their venues, a compliance burden, but the exemption for short-term debt and initial offerings limits the scope. Their position in the bill is largely administrative.
